John Bell. John Stewart Bell was an Irish physicist who lived from 1928 to 1990. He developed Bell's inequality, a mathematical statement that fundamentally challenged the foundations of quantum mechanics. His 1964 theorem showed that no local realist theory could reproduce all predictions of quantum mechanics, forcing physicists to confront whether quantum entanglement violates locality, causality, or realism itself. Bell's work transformed the philosophical interpretation of quantum mechanics from academic debate into experimentally testable physics.

Bell was born in Belfast, Northern Ireland, in 1928 and studied physics and mathematics at Queen's University Belfast. He developed Bell's inequality in 1964 while at CERN—the European Organization for Nuclear Research—in Geneva. This work began as a response to the EPR paradox proposed by Albert Einstein and collaborators. Bell's theorem proved that any local hidden-variable theory must obey his inequality. Quantum mechanics violates it, meaning either locality or realism must be abandoned.

The inequality is mathematically elegant. For measurements on entangled particles, the quantum predictions exceed the classical bound by at most a factor of the square root of two, a result independent of the specific quantum system. Bell's work inspired decades of increasingly precise experiments to test his inequality. Most confirmed quantum mechanics and rejected local realism, though loopholes remained until 2015.

Bell authored the influential essay "On the Problem of Hidden Variables in Quantum Mechanics" in 1966 and later wrote accessibly about quantum foundations in "Speakable and Unspeakable in Quantum Mechanics" published in 1987. He worked at CERN for most of his career, contributing to both theoretical quantum mechanics and accelerator physics.

He died in 1990, shortly before experimental evidence strongly supported his predictions. In 2022, the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for experiments closing loopholes in Bell tests he had inspired. His humble demeanor and philosophical insights made him unique among theoretical physicists. He communicated quantum foundations ideas with unusual clarity and accessibility to both specialists and general audiences.

Bell's inequality is the mathematical result that bears his name and launched experimental quantum foundations. His work illuminated quantum entanglement, showing it enables correlations impossible in classical physics. He clarified quantum mechanics by proving it incompatible with local realism. His investigations were motivated by Albert Einstein's EPR paradox about hidden variables.
